title: Chain Homotopy and the Homotopy Category

items.title: A graded morphism of chain complexes
The Hom complex of chain complexes
The Hom-complex differential squares to zero
items.strategy: Expand the graded commutator differential twice and group the four terms. The middle pair cancels by sign, while the outer pair vanishes because both source and target differentials square to zero.

items.title: Zero cocycles in the Hom complex are chain maps
items.strategy: For a degree-zero graded morphism u, the cocycle condition is exactly d_D u - u d_C = 0. Rewrite that equality componentwise to recover the usual chain-map commutative squares.

items.title: A chain homotopy
A null-homotopic chain map
Chain homotopy is an equivalence relation
items.strategy: Use the zero degree-one family for reflexivity, negate a chosen homotopy for symmetry, and add chosen homotopies for transitivity. Each case is a direct check against the defining equation f - g = d s + s d.

items.title: Chain homotopy is compatible with addition and composition
items.strategy: Add homotopies componentwise to treat sums, and whisker a homotopy by composable chain maps on the left and right. The chain-map identities move the differentials past the whiskered maps and leave the same homotopy formula.

items.title: Null-homotopic maps form a two-sided additive ideal
items.strategy: The zero map is null-homotopic via the zero homotopy, sums of null-homotopic maps stay null-homotopic by componentwise addition, and whiskering on either side stays null-homotopic by the previous lemma.

items.title: Chain-homotopic maps induce the same map on homology
items.strategy: If f - g = d s + s d and z is a cycle, then (f - g)(z) = d(s z) is a boundary. In the categorical proof the same equation factors through the cycle kernel, the boundary image, and the homology quotient to show H_n(f) = H_n(g).

items.title: Null-homotopic maps induce zero on homology
items.strategy: Apply the theorem to a map f homotopic to the zero chain map. The induced map agrees with the induced map of zero, hence is zero in every degree.

items.title: A chain homotopy equivalence
A contractible complex
A chain homotopy equivalence is a quasi-isomorphism
items.strategy: If g f and f g are homotopic to the relevant identities, the previous theorem gives H(g) H(f) = 1 and H(f) H(g) = 1. Therefore each H_n(f) is an isomorphism, which is exactly the quasi-isomorphism condition.

items.title: A contractible complex is acyclic
items.strategy: A contractible complex is homotopy equivalent to the zero complex. The previous theorem makes that equivalence a quasi-isomorphism, so every homology object of the complex is zero.

items.title: Homotopy classes of chain maps
Composition of homotopy classes is well defined
items.strategy: Replace one representative at a time. The difference between the two composites is obtained by whiskering a null-homotopic map, so it is again null-homotopic and the class of the composite does not depend on the choices.

items.title: The homotopy category of chain complexes
The homotopy category is additive
items.strategy: Each hom-set is the quotient of an abelian group by the subgroup of null-homotopic maps, so addition descends. The zero complex and degreewise biproducts already exist in Ch(A), and the ideal property shows their universal maps descend to K(A).

items.title: The canonical functor from complexes to the homotopy category is additive
items.strategy: The quotient functor is identity on objects and sends a chain map to its homotopy class. Because addition on hom-sets is defined by quotienting the additive hom-groups of Ch(A), the functor preserves zero maps, sums, and finite biproduct structure.

items.title: Homology factors uniquely through the homotopy category
items.strategy: The equality of homology maps for homotopic chain maps makes H_n constant on homotopy classes, so H_n descends along the quotient functor. Uniqueness follows because the quotient functor is identity on objects and surjective on each hom-group by definition.

items.title: Zero homology does not make an object zero in the homotopy category
items.strategy: An object is zero in K(A) exactly when its identity morphism is the zero class, which is to say exactly when the identity is null-homotopic. Thus contractibility characterizes zero objects in K(A), while acyclicity alone only says that the homology functors vanish.

items.title: Hom in the homotopy category is zero-degree homology of the Hom complex
items.strategy: Degree-zero cocycles in the Hom complex are exactly chain maps, and degree-zero boundaries are exactly differences of chain-homotopic maps. Quotienting cocycles by boundaries therefore identifies H^0(Hom(C, D)) with homotopy classes of chain maps.

items.title: The shift of a chain complex
The shifted differential squares to zero
items.strategy: Compose two shifted differentials. The sign contributes (-1)^(2k), so the composite is exactly the old differential squared on the shifted degree and therefore vanishes.

items.title: Shifted chain maps and shifted chain homotopies
Shift is an additive autoequivalence of the complex and homotopy categories
items.strategy: On Ch(A), the formulas for the shifted differentials and shifted maps give functors [k] and [-k] whose composites are the identity on the nose. Compatibility of shifted homotopies with the original homotopy relation shows the same formulas descend to K(A).

items.title: Homology of a shift is shifted homology
items.strategy: The n-cycles and n-boundaries of C[k] are the same underlying subobjects as the (n - k)-cycles and (n - k)-boundaries of C because the shifted differential differs only by the sign (-1)^k. The quotient defining homology is therefore the corresponding old homology object.

items.title: Shift preserves homotopy equivalences, contractibility, and quasi-isomorphisms
items.strategy: Shift a chosen homotopy inverse and the chosen homotopies to preserve homotopy equivalence. Contractibility is the special case of an object homotopy equivalent to zero, and the homology-shift formula transfers quasi-isomorphisms degree by degree.

items.title: Suspension and desuspension of a chain complex
A degreewise split exact complex with compatible splittings is contractible
items.strategy: Use the chosen compatible splittings to define degree-one maps s_n explicitly. The compatibility equation is exactly what makes d s + s d equal the identity, so the complex is contractible by definition.

items.title: A bounded below acyclic complex of projective objects is contractible when its cycle epimorphisms split
items.strategy: For an acyclic bounded-below complex, each short exact sequence 0 -> Z_n -> C_n -> Z_{n-1} -> 0 starts at a genuine bottom degree. The chosen splittings of the cycle epimorphisms assemble inductively into the compatible splittings required by the previous lemma.

items.title: A bounded above acyclic complex of injective objects is contractible when its cycle monomorphisms split
items.strategy: Pass to the opposite abelian category, where a bounded-above chain complex becomes a bounded-below chain complex and injective objects become projective. Apply the previous theorem there and translate the resulting contraction back.

items.title: Homotopy equivalence is an equivalence relation on complexes
items.strategy: The identity map is its own homotopy inverse, the inverse data swaps under symmetry, and the composite of chosen homotopy inverses is again a homotopy inverse because chain homotopy is compatible with composition.

items.title: A chain isomorphism is a chain homotopy equivalence
items.strategy: A chain isomorphism already has an inverse chain map. The inverse composites are literally the identity chain maps, so the homotopy-equivalence conditions hold with the zero homotopies.

items.title: FALSE: chain-homotopic maps are equal as chain maps
items.strategy: The companion exhibits distinct chain maps whose difference is d s + s d for a nonzero homotopy. Equality is only forced after passing to homotopy classes in K(A), not inside Ch(A) itself.

items.title: FALSE: every acyclic complex is contractible
items.strategy: The companion's nonsplit-extension complex has zero homology but no contraction. This is exactly the distinction the page preserves between acyclic and contractible objects.

items.title: FALSE: every quasi-isomorphism is a chain homotopy equivalence
items.strategy: The zero map from the companion's acyclic but noncontractible complex to the zero complex is a quasi-isomorphism. If it had a homotopy inverse, that complex would be contractible, contradicting the earlier criterion.

items.title: FALSE: the homotopy category is obtained by identifying quasi-isomorphisms with identities
items.strategy: K(A) quotients by chain homotopy classes of maps, while inverting quasi-isomorphisms is a later localization step. Conflating the two would erase the distinction between the homotopy category and the derived category.

items.title: FALSE: the shift of a complex keeps the same differential with no sign
items.strategy: Without the factor (-1)^k, the shifted differential need not square to zero when k is odd. The sign is also the convention that keeps the later cone and rotation formulas consistent.

title: Chain Homotopy and the Homotopy Category - Examples

items.title: A contracting homotopy for the two-term identity complex
items.strategy: Use the two-term complex 0 -> A -> A -> 0 with the identity differential, place A in abelian groups, and write the degree-one map whose only nonzero component is the identity. A direct calculation gives d s + s d = 1.

items.title: Two homotopic maps with different components
items.strategy: On the contractible two-term identity complex, compare the identity map with the zero map. The explicit contracting homotopy shows they are homotopic even though their degree-zero components are visibly different.

items.title: The Hom complex of two two-term complexes
items.strategy: Choose two small two-term complexes in Ab, list the graded maps degree by degree, and compute the commutator differential explicitly. The example makes the degree convention and the zero-cocycle condition concrete.

items.title: A split exact complex and its contraction
items.strategy: Take a three-term split exact sequence of abelian groups, view it as a complex, and write the compatible splittings and the resulting contraction degree by degree. This is the template behind the general contractibility criterion.

items.title: An acyclic noncontractible complex from a nonsplit extension
items.strategy: View a nonsplit short exact sequence 0 -> A -> B -> C -> 0 as a three-term complex. Exactness makes it acyclic, while a contraction would split the sequence and contradict the choice of a nonsplit extension.

items.title: A quasi-isomorphism with no homotopy inverse
items.strategy: Use the zero map from the companion's acyclic noncontractible complex to the zero complex. It is a quasi-isomorphism because both homology objects vanish, but a homotopy inverse would make the source contractible.

items.title: Shifting a three-term complex with all signs
items.strategy: Write a short three-term complex and then compute its shift term by term, including the sign on every shifted differential and the induced reindexing of homology. This pins down the convention used later for cones and triangles.

items.title: Homotopy classes as H-zero of a Hom complex
items.strategy: Continue the explicit Hom-complex computation from the previous example, identify its degree-zero cocycles and degree-zero boundaries, and compare the resulting quotient with the homotopy classes of chain maps between the same complexes.
